sections.title: PART 1: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING ESSENTIALS & SDLC MODELS

topics.title: Software Engineering & The Software Crisis
topics.explanation:
-Software Engineering: Software engineering is a disciplined approach to building reliable software on time and within budget.
-Software Crisis: The software crisis refers to common problems where projects run late, exceed budgets, and carry bugs.
topics.tldr: Software Engineering মানে সময় ও বাজেটের মধ্যে ভালো সফটওয়্যার বানানো। সফটওয়্যার কখনো ঘুণ ধরে নষ্ট হয় না, বারবার ভুলভাল চেঞ্জ করলে নষ্ট হয়।
keyPoints: Software engineering focuses on practical, cost-effective methods to deliver working systems.
Software deteriorates rather than wearing out mechanically.
Fixing bugs early during requirements is much cheaper than fixing them during maintenance.
Maintenance takes up most of the total software lifecycle cost.
Adding more people to a late project usually delays it further.

comparisons.title: Computer Science vs Software Engineering
rows: Cost of finding and fixing defects

traps.statement: Does software wear out over time like hardware?
traps.explanation: No. Hardware wears out physically. Software deteriorates when new changes introduce bugs.

traps.statement: Can you speed up a delayed project by adding more developers?
traps.explanation: No. New people need training and increase communication overhead, slowing things down.

topics.title: Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)
topics.explanation: -Software Development Life Cycle : SDLC is the step-by-step workflow used to plan, create, test, and maintain software. It ensures software is built systematically from start to finish.
topics.tldr: SDLC steps: Requirements → Design → Coding → Testing → Deployment → Maintenance.
keyPoints: Requirements: Understand what the user needs and what constraints exist.
Design: Plan the system structure, database models, and interfaces.
Implementation: Write code and combine modules.
Testing: Check that features work and find bugs.
Deployment: Release the working software to users.
Maintenance: Fix bugs, handle environment changes, and add small enhancements.

traps.statement: Does SDLC end right after deployment?
traps.explanation: No. Maintenance is the longest phase and lasts as long as the software is in use.

topics.title: SDLC Process Models: Waterfall, V-Model & Prototyping
topics.explanation: Different SDLC models organize work in different ways.
topics.tldr: Waterfall ধাপে ধাপে সোজা চলে, V-Model প্রতিটা ধাপে টেস্টিং করায়, আর Prototyping দিয়ে কনফিউজিং আইডিয়া ক্লিয়ার করা হয়।
keyPoints: Waterfall: Linear and strict; hard to go back once a phase finishes.
V-Model: Every development step has a matching testing step.
Prototyping: Best when the client is not sure what they want.

traps.statement: Can Waterfall easily handle changing customer requirements?
traps.explanation: No. Waterfall assumes stable requirements; changes require restarting or costly rework.

topics.title: Agile Principles
topics.explanation: -Agile: Agile is an iterative way of building software in short cycles called iterations or sprints.
topics.tldr: Agile-এ time আর budget ফিক্সড, কিন্তু requirement flex করা যায়; কাজ চলে ১-৪ সপ্তাহের sprint-এ।
keyPoints: Agile works best when requirements change frequently.
Delivers working software in short cycles (1 to 4 weeks).
Values working code and customer collaboration over rigid plans and paperwork.
Teams are cross-functional and self-organizing.

traps.statement: Does Agile mean you should never write documentation?
traps.explanation: No. Agile simply avoids useless paperwork, keeping documentation light and useful.

topics.title: Scrum
topics.explanation: -Scrum: Scrum is a popular Agile framework. Work is split into fixed time periods called Sprints (1 to 4 weeks). It defines three roles, four main meetings, and three core artifacts.
topics.tldr: Scrum চলে ছোট ছোট sprint-এ; Product Owner কাজ ঠিক করে, Scrum Master blocker সরায়, আর Dev Team কোড বানায়।
keyPoints: Product Owner: Decides feature priorities and owns the Product Backlog.
Scrum Master: Ensures the team follows Scrum.
Development Team: Cross-functional group that builds the software.
Artifacts: Product Backlog (all items), Sprint Backlog (current items), and Working Increment.
Ceremonies: Sprint Planning, Daily Standup, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective.

traps.statement: Can the Product Owner add new items mid-sprint?
traps.explanation: No. The sprint backlog is locked during the sprint. New ideas wait for the next sprint.

topics.title: Extreme Programming (XP)
topics.explanation: -Extreme Programming: XP is an agile framework focused on clean engineering practices. It emphasizes pair programming, test-first coding, refactoring, and regular customer feedback.
topics.tldr: XP হলো engineering practice-focused agile method; সবচেয়ে পপুলার হাইব্রিড হলো Scrum + XP।
keyPoints: Pair Programming: Two developers share one computer; one types (Driver), one reviews (Navigator).
Test-Driven Development (TDD): Write failing automated tests first, then write code to pass them.
Refactoring: Clean up internal code design without changing what it does outside.
Collective Ownership: Any developer on the team can edit any piece of code.
Continuous Integration: Code is integrated and tested multiple times a day.

traps.statement: In Pair Programming, do both developers write code separately?
traps.explanation: No. Both work on one machine; one types while the other reviews logic and plans ahead.

topics.title: Software Requirements Engineering
topics.explanation: -Software Requirements Engineering: SRE is the process of discovering, analyzing, documenting, validating, and managing what a software system needs to do.
topics.tldr: Requirements Engineering = বুঝে নেওয়া, analyze করা, document করা এবং validate করা যে software-এ কী কী দরকার।
keyPoints: Requirements describe what the system must provide and the constraints it must follow.
Good requirements should be clear, consistent, testable, and understandable.
Requirements Engineering helps reduce expensive misunderstandings later in development.
Requirements can change as business needs and user expectations change.

comparisons.title: Requirement vs Design
rows: How the system will do it

traps.statement: Is a specific technical implementation always a requirement?
traps.explanation: No. A requirement describes the needed behavior or constraint; implementation details belong to design unless explicitly required.

topics.title: Requirement Elicitation
topics.explanation: -Elicitation: Requirement elicitation is the process of collecting requirements from stakeholders and understanding their actual needs.
topics.tldr: Elicitation মানে stakeholder-এর কাছ থেকে আসল requirements বের করে আনা।
keyPoints: Common techniques include interviews, questionnaires, observation, workshops, brainstorming, and prototyping.
Stakeholders can include customers, users, managers, domain experts, and development teams.
The goal is to discover both stated requirements and hidden needs.
Prototypes can help clarify unclear or difficult requirements.

comparisons.title: Common Elicitation Techniques
rows: Clarifying unclear UI or feature expectations

traps.statement: Should requirements always come only from the client?
traps.explanation: No. Different stakeholders and actual users can reveal different requirements and constraints.

topics.title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
topics.explanation:
-Functional requirements:It define what the system should do.
-Non-functional requirements: It define how well the system should do it, covering quality traits like speed, security, and availability.
topics.tldr: Functional = system features; Non-functional = quality and performance.
keyPoints: Functional: Specific features, user actions, and system responses (e.g., login, payment).
Non-Functional: Performance, availability, maintainability, response time, and security.
Non-functional requirements heavily influence system architecture and hardware choices.
Baseline: An agreed set of requirements that can only change through formal approval.

traps.statement: Is security purely a functional requirement?
traps.explanation: No. Security is a non-functional quality trait that leads to functional features like login pages.

topics.title: User Stories & Acceptance Criteria
topics.explanation:
-User Story: A user story describes a feature from the user's perspective. 
-Acceptance criteria: It defines the conditions that must be satisfied for the story to be considered complete.
topics.tldr: User Story বলে user কী চায়; Acceptance Criteria বলে কখন feature-টাকে complete বলা যাবে।
keyPoints: A common user story format is: As a [user], I want [goal], so that [benefit].
Acceptance criteria should be specific, testable, and understandable.
Acceptance criteria help developers and testers agree on expected behavior.
A story is not complete just because the code has been written.

comparisons.title: User Story vs Acceptance Criteria
rows: Valid reset link allows password change

traps.statement: Does a user story describe exactly how developers must implement a feature?
traps.explanation: No. It describes the user need and expected value; implementation details are usually left to the development team.

topics.title: Requirement Analysis, Prioritization & Validation
topics.explanation: Simple flow: Collect Requirements → Analyze → Check Feasibility & Conflicts → Set Priority → Validate Requirements → Final Requirements
topics.tldr: Requirements analyze করে conflict/feasibility দেখা হয়, priority দেওয়া হয় এবং শেষে validate করা হয়।
keyPoints: Analysis identifies ambiguity, conflicts, dependencies, feasibility issues, and missing requirements.
Prioritization helps teams decide what should be delivered first.
Business value, risk, urgency, dependencies, and technical feasibility can influence priority.
Requirement validation checks correctness, completeness, consistency, feasibility, and testability.
Changing requirements should be tracked and communicated rather than handled informally.

comparisons.title: Analysis vs Validation
rows: What do these requirements mean and how do they fit together?
Are these requirements clear, complete, feasible, and testable?

traps.statement: Is requirement validation the same as testing the finished application?
traps.explanation: No. Requirement validation happens before implementation to ensure the requirements themselves are correct and usable.

topics.title: Software Design
topics.explanation:
Good software design keeps parts independent and easy to understand.
-Cohesion: Cohesion refers to how focused a single module is on doing one job well.
-Coupling: Coupling refers to how much different modules depend on each other.
topics.tldr: Software design-এর গোল একটাই: High Cohesion (একটা module একটাই কাজ করবে) আর Low Coupling (একে অন্যের ওপর কম depend করবে)।
keyPoints: High Cohesion: A module has one clear responsibility and does it well.
Low Coupling: Modules stay independent and connect only through clean interfaces.
High coupling makes code fragile; changing one module breaks others.
Good UI design keeps interfaces consistent and gives users clear control.

traps.statement: Is high coupling good for software design?
traps.explanation: No. High coupling causes domino-effect bugs whenever you make a change.

topics.title: Software Quality Assurance VS Quality Control
topics.explanation:
-Software Quality Assurance: QA focuses on improving processes to prevent defects before they happen. 
-Software Quality Control: QC focuses on checking the software to find defects after or during development. In simple terms, QA prevents problems, while QC finds problems.
topics.tldr: QA = Process improve করে defect prevent করা। QC = Software check করে defect খুঁজে বের করা।
keyPoints: Quality Assurance (QA) is process-oriented and focuses on preventing defects.
Quality Control (QC) is product-oriented and focuses on finding defects.
QA can define coding standards, create development guidelines, review processes, and ensure developers follow proper requirements before defects occur.
QC checks whether the software meets quality requirements.
Testing is one of the main activities used in Quality Control.

comparisons.title: Quality Assurance vs Quality Control
rows: Check the quality of the software

traps.statement: Are Quality Assurance and Quality Control the same?
traps.explanation: No. QA focuses on preventing defects by improving processes, while QC focuses on finding defects by checking and testing the software.

topics.title: Testing Fundamentals: Verification vs Validation
topics.explanation:
-Software Testing: Testing is running a system to catch defects before delivery. 
-Verification: Verification checks if the software meets its technical specs. 
-Validation: Validation checks if it actually meets user needs.
topics.tldr: Verification কোড চেক করে, Validation ইউজারের আসল দরকার মেলায়
keyPoints: Verification: Checking code, designs, and specs during development.
Validation: Checking the final working software against client needs.
Testing reveals bugs; it cannot prove that zero bugs exist.
Regression Testing: Re-running tests to make sure new code didn't break old features.
Smoke Testing: Quick run to check if the basic build runs before detailed testing.

comparisons.title: Verification vs Validation
rows: Are we building the product right?
Are we building the right product?
Executing the application with real scenarios

traps.statement: Should only the original developer test their own code?
traps.explanation: No. Developers have blind spots; independent testers test aggressively to find hidden bugs.

topics.title: Testing Strategies
topics.explanation: Simple Flow: Unit Testing → Integration Testing → System Testing → Acceptance Testing.
topics.tldr: Testing শুরু হয় Unit দিয়ে, এরপর Integration, System এবং শেষে UAT; টেস্টের প্রয়োজনে সাহায্য নেওয়া হয় Driver (caller) আর Stub (callee) দিয়ে।
keyPoints: Unit Testing: Tests individual functions or classes in isolation to catch bugs early.
Integration Testing: Tests how different modules work and communicate together.
System Testing: Tests the entire assembled application in a realistic environment.
UAT (User Acceptance Testing): Final check by actual users to confirm it solves business needs.
Driver: A temporary dummy program that calls and sends test data to a module.
Stub: A temporary dummy program that simulates an unbuilt child module.

traps.statement: What is the difference between a Driver and a Stub?
traps.explanation: A Driver acts as the caller module. A Stub acts as the called module being simulated.

topics.title: Common Black-Box Testing Techniques
topics.explanation: -Black-Box Testing:Black-box techniques design test cases from requirements and expected behavior without examining the internal implementation.
topics.tldr: Black-box testing-এ code না দেখে input-এর important groups আর boundary ধরে test case বানানো হয়।
keyPoints: Equivalence Partitioning: Divide inputs into groups expected to behave similarly and test representative values.
Boundary Value Analysis: Test values at, just below, and just above important boundaries.
Decision Table Testing: Test combinations of conditions and resulting actions.
Use-case Testing: Test realistic user workflows from start to finish.

comparisons.title: Equivalence Partitioning vs Boundary Value Analysis
rows: Divide input into valid and invalid classes
Age 18-60 → test one value from valid and invalid ranges
Focus on edges of valid ranges

traps.statement: Does Boundary Value Analysis mainly focus on random middle values?
traps.explanation: No. It focuses on values at and around the boundaries where defects commonly occur.

topics.title: Test Cases, Bugs, Severity & Priority
topics.explanation: -Test-case: A test case defines inputs, conditions, actions, and expected results for checking a requirement. -Bugs: Bugs are defects where actual behavior differs from expected behavior.
topics.tldr: Test Case বলে কীভাবে feature check করবে; Severity বলে bug কতটা damaging, Priority বলে কত দ্রুত fix করা দরকার।
keyPoints: A test case commonly includes preconditions, test steps, input data, expected result, and actual result.
A defect is identified when actual behavior does not match the expected behavior.
Severity measures the technical or business impact of a defect.
Priority measures how urgently the defect should be fixed.
A low-severity defect can still have high priority when it affects an important visible feature.

comparisons.title: Severity vs Priority
rows: How serious the defect impact is
How urgently it should be fixed
How badly does it affect the system?
How soon should we fix it?

traps.statement: Are Severity and Priority the same thing?
traps.explanation: No. Severity measures impact; Priority determines urgency.

topics.title: Smoke, Sanity & Regression Testing
topics.explanation:
-Smoke Testing: Smoke testing checks whether a build is stable enough for deeper testing. 
-Sanity Testing: Sanity testing checks a focused change. 
-Regression Testing: Regression testing checks that existing functionality still works after changes.
topics.tldr: Smoke = build ঠিক আছে কিনা; Sanity = specific change ঠিক আছে কিনা; Regression = পুরোনো feature ভাঙেনি কিনা।
keyPoints: Smoke Testing: Broad and shallow testing of critical functionality on a new build.
Sanity Testing: Narrow testing focused on a particular change or fix.
Regression Testing: Re-running existing tests after changes to detect unintended breakage.
Regression testing can be automated to provide faster feedback.

traps.statement: Is Smoke Testing the same as Regression Testing?
traps.explanation: No. Smoke testing checks whether a build is stable enough for further testing, while regression checks whether existing functionality was broken by changes.

topics.title: White-Box Testing
topics.explanation: -White-Box Testing:White-Box testing looks directly inside the code to check internal paths and logic.
topics.tldr: White-box টেস্ট করে ভেতরের কোড; Black-box ভেতরের কোড না দেখেই শুধু ইনপুট-আউটপুট মিলিয়ে দেখে।
keyPoints: White-Box Testing: Tests internal code paths, branches, conditions, and loops.

comparisons.title: White-Box vs Black-Box Testing
rows: Full view of internal source code
No view of internal source code

traps.statement: Does re-running an old code path count as a new independent path?
traps.explanation: No. An independent path must cover at least one brand new code condition or edge.

topics.title: Git & Version Control in Practice
topics.explanation:
-Git: Git is a distributed version control system where each developer keeps a full copy of the project history locally. Common actions include staging changes, committing snapshots, branching, and syncing with a remote server.
-GitHub: GitHub is a cloud-based hosting service for Git repositories that lets developers store, track, and collaborate on software projects.
topics.tldr: Git লোকালি কোডের চেঞ্জ ট্র্যাক করে আর GitHub ক্লাউডে টিমের সাথে শেয়ার করে; মেইন ফ্লো: Working Tree → add → commit → push।
keyPoints: Working Directory: The local folder where you actively edit files.
Staging Area (git add): Picks and prepares specific changes for the next commit.
Local Repository (git commit): Saves a permanent snapshot of changes on your machine.
Remote Repository (git push): Backs up and shares local commits to cloud hosts like GitHub.
Branches (git branch): Safe, isolated spaces to build features without touching main code.
Merging (git merge): Combines code and commits from one branch into another.
Fetch vs Pull: git fetch only downloads remote history; git pull downloads and merges it instantly.
Merge Conflicts: Happen when two branches edit the same lines, requiring manual fixes.

git commit -m "Fix login validation"

traps.statement: Does Git need GitHub to work?
traps.explanation: No. Git works completely offline on your local computer.

topics.title: CI/CD & DevOps Automation
topics.explanation:
-CI: Continuous Integration automatically tests and builds code as soon as developers commit it. 
-CD:Continuous Delivery keeps the software ready to release at any time. Continuous Deployment automatically ships every passing update directly to users.
topics.tldr: CI automates testing; Continuous Delivery prepares releases; Continuous Deployment releases automatically.
keyPoints: CI catches bugs early by building and testing code on every commit.
Continuous Delivery requires a human click to deploy to production.
Continuous Deployment releases to production automatically without manual approval.
DevOps unites development and IT operations through automated pipelines.

traps.statement: Are Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment the exact same thing?
traps.explanation: No. Continuous Delivery needs manual sign-off; Continuous Deployment ships automatically.

topics.title: Technical Debt, Code Review & Scalability
topics.explanation:
-Technical Debt: A quick or messy solution that creates more work later. 
-Scalability: A system's ability to handle more users or data as it grows.
topics.tldr: Technical debt is tomorrow's rework for today's shortcuts. Scale vertically (bigger machine) or horizontally (more machines).
keyPoints: Technical Debt: Caused by rushed deadlines, skipping tests, or postponing refactoring.
Code Reviews: Team members review pull requests to catch bugs and keep code clean.
Vertical Scaling: Upgrading CPU or RAM on an existing server.
Horizontal Scaling: Adding more server instances behind a load balancer.
Monolith vs Microservices: Monoliths are simpler to start with; Microservices split domains into separate services.

traps.statement: Should every new application start as microservices?
traps.explanation: No. Microservices add distributed network complexity. Most apps should start as a modular monolith.

topics.title: Core Design Principles: DRY, KISS, YAGNI & SOLID
topics.explanation: Basic coding principles keep code clean, simple, and easy to change. DRY avoids duplication, KISS keeps logic simple, YAGNI prevents building unused features, and SOLID provides five core object-oriented rules.
topics.tldr: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself), KISS (Keep It Simple), YAGNI (Build Only What You Need Now), and SOLID guide clean OOP.
keyPoints: DRY: Avoid repeating the same logic in multiple places.
KISS: Keep code simple; avoid unnecessary layers.
YAGNI: Do not write code for features you might only need in the future.
Single Responsibility (SRP): A class should have only one reason to change.
Open/Closed (OCP): Open for extension, closed for modification.
Liskov Substitution (LSP): Subclasses must be swappable for their parent class without issues.
Interface Segregation (ISP): Keep interfaces small and specific.
Dependency Inversion (DIP): Depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.

codeSnippets.explanation: Applying the Single Responsibility Principle by splitting database tasks from email tasks.

traps.statement: Does DRY mean combining any two code blocks that look similar?
traps.explanation: No. Only combine them if they represent the exact same business rule, not just accidental similarity.

topics.title: High-Yield Interview Questions
topics.explanation: Common conceptual questions asked in technical software engineering interviews.

questions.question: Q1: Why is fixing a bug in maintenance much more expensive than in requirements?
questions.answer: Because a late bug requires redesigning, rewriting code, re-testing multiple components, and pushing patches to production.

questions.question: Q2: What is the key difference between Verification and Validation?
questions.answer: Verification checks if the product matches technical specs ('Are we building the product right?'). Validation checks if it solves user needs ('Are we building the right product?').

questions.question: Q3: What are High Cohesion and Low Coupling?
questions.answer: High Cohesion means a class has one clear, focused job. Low Coupling means modules stay independent with minimal shared connections.

questions.question: Q4: What are the three roles in Scrum?
questions.answer: Product Owner (manages backlog priorities), Scrum Master (removes blockers and guards the process), and the Development Team (builds the increments).

questions.question: Q5: What is a software baseline in SCM?
questions.answer: A formally reviewed and approved version of a document or codebase that requires formal approval to modify.

questions.question: Q6: What is the difference between White-Box and Black-Box testing?
questions.answer: White-Box tests internal paths and code structure directly. Black-Box tests inputs and outputs from the outside without checking code.

questions.question: Q7: What is Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment?
questions.answer: Continuous Delivery keeps code ready to release with a manual release trigger. Continuous Deployment automatically ships every passing commit to production.

questions.question: Q8: What is the difference between Severity and Priority?
questions.answer: Severity measures how much a defect impacts the system or business. Priority measures how urgently the defect should be fixed.

questions.question: Q9: What is the difference between a User Story and Acceptance Criteria?
questions.answer: A User Story describes a user's need and goal. Acceptance Criteria define the specific conditions that must be satisfied for the story to be considered complete.

questions.question: Q10: What is the difference between QA and Testing?
questions.answer: QA focuses on improving processes to prevent defects, while Testing focuses on executing software to discover defects.

topics.title: Quick Flashcards
topics.explanation: Fast recall flashcards for technical review.
topics.tldr: Quick-fire review cards covering SDLC, Agile, Requirements, Testing, and Architecture.

flashcards.question: What is Software Engineering?
flashcards.answer: A systematic and disciplined approach to developing, operating, and maintaining software.

flashcards.question: What is the Software Crisis?
flashcards.answer: Problems where software projects become late, expensive, difficult to maintain, or full of defects.

flashcards.question: What are the main phases of SDLC?
flashcards.answer: Requirements, Design, Implementation, Testing, Deployment, and Maintenance.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between Waterfall and Agile?
flashcards.answer: Waterfall follows sequential phases with stable requirements, while Agile develops software iteratively and adapts to changing requirements.

flashcards.question: What is a Sprint in Scrum?
flashcards.answer: A fixed time period, usually one to four weeks, during which a team creates a working product increment.

flashcards.question: What are the three main Scrum roles?
flashcards.answer: Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers or Development Team.

flashcards.question: What is the Product Backlog?
flashcards.answer: A prioritized list of all features, improvements, fixes, and work needed for the product.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between Functional and Non-Functional Requirements?
flashcards.answer: Functional requirements define what the system does, while non-functional requirements define how well the system performs.

flashcards.question: What is a Non-Functional Requirement example?
flashcards.answer: The system must respond to user requests within two seconds.

flashcards.question: What is High Cohesion?
flashcards.answer: A module or class has one clear and focused responsibility.

flashcards.question: What is Low Coupling?
flashcards.answer: Modules have minimal dependency on each other, making changes easier and safer.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between Verification and Validation?
flashcards.answer: Verification asks whether we are building the product right, while Validation asks whether we are building the right product.

flashcards.question: What is Unit Testing?
flashcards.answer: Testing individual functions, methods, classes, or components in isolation.

flashcards.question: What is Integration Testing?
flashcards.answer: Testing whether different modules or components communicate and work correctly together.

flashcards.question: What is System Testing?
flashcards.answer: Testing the complete integrated software system as a whole.

flashcards.question: What is UAT?
flashcards.answer: User Acceptance Testing is testing performed by users or clients to confirm that the software meets business requirements.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between a Driver and a Stub?
flashcards.answer: A Driver simulates a calling parent module, while a Stub simulates a called child module.

flashcards.question: What is White-Box Testing?
flashcards.answer: Testing internal code structure, execution paths, branches, conditions, and logic.

flashcards.question: What is Black-Box Testing?
flashcards.answer: Testing software functionality through inputs and outputs without examining internal source code.

flashcards.question: What is Regression Testing?
flashcards.answer: Re-running tests to ensure new changes have not broken previously working features.

flashcards.question: What is Smoke Testing?
flashcards.answer: A quick initial test to verify that the most important features of a software build are working.

flashcards.question: Does testing prove software has zero bugs?
flashcards.answer: No. Testing can reveal the presence of defects but cannot prove that software is completely bug-free.

flashcards.question: What is Git?
flashcards.answer: A distributed version control system used to track changes and manage source code history.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
flashcards.answer: Git is a version control system, while GitHub is a cloud platform for hosting and collaborating on Git repositories.

flashcards.question: What is a Git Commit?
flashcards.answer: A saved snapshot of staged changes in the local repository.

flashcards.question: What is a Git Branch?
flashcards.answer: An independent line of development used to work on features without directly changing the main branch.

flashcards.question: What is Continuous Integration?
flashcards.answer: Automatically building and testing code changes frequently to detect integration problems early.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
flashcards.answer: Continuous Delivery keeps software ready for release with manual approval, while Continuous Deployment automatically releases passing changes to production.

flashcards.question: What is Technical Debt?
flashcards.answer: The future cost of additional work caused by choosing a quick or messy solution instead of a better solution today.

flashcards.question: What does DRY mean?
flashcards.answer: Don't Repeat Yourself. Avoid duplicating the same knowledge or business logic in multiple places.

flashcards.question: What does KISS mean?
flashcards.answer: Keep It Simple. Prefer simple solutions over unnecessary complexity.

flashcards.question: What does YAGNI mean?
flashcards.answer: You Aren't Gonna Need It. Do not build features until they are actually needed.

flashcards.question: What is SRP in SOLID?
flashcards.answer: Single Responsibility Principle means a class should have one responsibility and one main reason to change.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between Vertical and Horizontal Scaling?
flashcards.answer: Vertical scaling increases resources on one server, while horizontal scaling adds more servers or instances.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between a Monolith and Microservices?
flashcards.answer: A monolith is one unified application, while microservices divide functionality into independent services.

traps.statement: Running all tests guarantees there are zero bugs left in the code.
traps.explanation: Testing only shows that bugs exist, never that software is 100% bug-free.

traps.statement: Adding more developers to a late project helps finish it on time.
traps.explanation: Adding people adds communication delays and training time, slowing work down further.
